stages.answer_line: Recommended opening definition: Jainism (Jina-centred path of many-sided reality and liberation) is a pluralist realism in which anekāntavāda (doctrine of many-sided reality) holds that enduring dravya (substance) possesses guṇa (qualities) and changing paryāya (modes).

stages.answer_line: Jaina bondage begins when āsrava (influx) brings karmic matter into the soul and bandha (bondage) binds it; saṃvara (stoppage) and nirjarā (shedding) culminate in mokṣa (liberation).

stages.title: SAPTABHAṄGĪ SEVENFOLD BRANCH

pills.text: ABOUT OBJECT X, UNDER SPECIFIED STANDPOINT
IN SOME RESPECT, X IS NOT
SUCCESSIVELY, X IS AND IS NOT

sequence: ABOUT OBJECT X, UNDER SPECIFIED STANDPOINT / TIME / MODE
1 syād-asti → in some respect, X is
2 syān-nāsti → in some respect, X is not
3 syād-asti-nāsti → successively, X is and is not
4 syād-avaktavyaḥ → X is inexpressible under simultaneous demand

stages.answer_line: Saptabhaṅgī (sevenfold predication) expresses syādvāda (doctrine of conditional assertion) by qualifying every judgement through a standpoint, thereby avoiding both dogmatic absolutism and sceptical silence.

stages.answer_line: Final verdict: Jaina philosophy combines metaphysical pluralism, perspectival logic and ethical self-purification, but its coherence depends on showing that conditional predication preserves truth without collapsing into contradiction or relativism.

stages.answer_line: The charge that anekāntavāda (doctrine of many-sided reality) is self-refuting fails if its own claim is understood as standpoint-qualified rather than as an unqualified absolute denial of absolutes.

stages.answer_line: Jainism (Jina-centred path of many-sided reality and liberation) mediates between Cārvāka (Indian materialist school), Buddhist flux and Advaita (non-dualism) by defending a many-sided reality of enduring substances that genuinely undergo changing modes.
